articles.title: Wendy’s, struggling with beef prices and growing competition, gets a buyout offer
articles.summary: Wendy’s shares jumped more than 14% Wednesday after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores.
articles.body: Wendy’s shares jumped more than 14% Wednesday after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores. Peltz’s Trian Fund Management and several partners are offering Wendy’s $7.35 per share in cash, or a premium of nearly 19% over the stock’s closing price on Tuesday, in a deal that would take the company private. The offer values Wendy’s at $1.4 billion. Wendy’s, which is based in Dublin, Ohio, confirmed receipt of the unsolicited proposal in a statement Wednesday and said its board has formed an independent committee to evaluate it. At the end of last year, Wendy’s had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries. Wendy’s, founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald’s and Burger King, Wendy’s launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where’s the beef?” ad campaign. But as the fast-food market grew even more competitive and rival burger-focused chains like In-N-Out and Five Guys expanded, Wendy’s fell behind. Wendy’s share of U.S. burger chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% last year, according to Technomic, a market research company. In recent years, inflation has also hurt Wendy’s and other U.S. fast-food chains, who have seen traffic from lower-income consumers fall as they raised prices to combat rising labor, food and packaging costs. Wendy’s said Wednesday it is moving “with urgency” to rebuild its menu with a focus on quality and improve marketing and store operations. Wendy’s hired Bob Wright, who formerly led Potbelly, as its president and CEO in May. He’s the fourth CEO to lead the company since 2024. Wendy’s has been closing outdated U.S. restaurants so it can focus on its more profitable locations. The company closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and said earlier this year that it planned to shutter up to 358 locations in 2026. Then, last month, one of the largest U.S. franchisees for Wendy’s filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain tried to terminate its franchise agreement. Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group operates 314 Wendy’s restaurants in 15 states. In a letter to the company’s board of directors, Peltz said going private “will deliver the best outcome for the broader stakeholder base.” “Wendy’s sits at a critical juncture,” Peltz wrote. “The external environment has become increasingly challenging given the significant pressures on the U.S. consumer, economic uncertainty, persistent commodity inflation and intensifying competition, particularly within the QSR (quick service restaurant) burger category.” Peltz has invested in companies from Procter & Gamble and Disney to DuPont. According to a regulatory document filed Wednesday, Trian’s stake in Wendy’s totals 16.3%. Peltz considered a take-private bid for Wendy’s in 2022 but told the company in January 2023 that he had decided against it, citing its improved business momentum, according to TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles. Charles said an independent special committee is expected to evaluate the proposal and both parties have entered into a confidentiality arrangement. “In our view, a take-private makes sense as Wendy’s turnaround is likely to be prolonged given the challenged state of the lower-income consumer and soft state of the quick service burger category,” Charles wrote Wednesday in a note to investors. Wendy’s is scheduled to report its quarterly financial results next week. Analysts expect the company to post earnings of 9 cents per share on sales of $531 million, according to FactSet. Shares rose 93 cents to $7.07 Wednesday. They have fallen 26% since the start of this year.

articles.title: North Koreans being recruited into forced labour in Russia, report says
articles.summary: Russian broker network recruiting North Korean labourers using student visas, Global Rights Compliance report says.
articles.body:
North Korean workers are being recruited into forced labour in Russia by a broker network using bogus student enrolments, according to a months-long investigation by an international law foundation.

The network brings North Koreans into Russia on student visas to skirt United Nations sanctions and labour law, as part of a state-sponsored work programme that helps fund Pyongyang’s ballistic missile development, according to the Global Rights Compliance report released on Thursday.

Operated by Russian businessman Vladimir Sokolov, labour-brokering platform KNDR.su markets North Korean workers to prospective Russian employers in agriculture, construction, industry and IT, charging a commission of 100,000-150,000 roubles ($1,240-$1,860) per placement, according to the Netherlands-based nonprofit.

In conversations with Global Rights Compliance investigators posing as prospective employers, Sokolov’s operations director, Ruslan Zhukov, said North Korean workers were enrolled in colleges they did not attend “to avoid the application of labour law”, the law foundation said.

Zhukov also described the workers being required to work 12 hours a day, six days a week, according to the report.

UN member states are prohibited from hosting North Korean workers under a 2017 UN Security Council resolution intended to deprive Pyongyang of funds for its nuclear weapons and missile programmes.

Despite UN sanctions, between 35,600 and 101,280 North Korean workers were based overseas in 2025, generating an estimated $450m-$800m for Pyongyang, according to an 11-country team that monitors sanctions enforcement.

Russia granted more than 36,000 visas to North Koreans in 2025, a fourfold increase from the previous year, almost all of which were officially for educational purposes.

Global Rights Compliance said the network also helped support Russia’s war effort in Ukraine, with Sokolov publicising at least two work sites with links to Moscow’s military-industrial complex.

Sokolov and Zhukov did not respond to requests for comment sent to Sokolov’s holding company, Black Horse, and KNDR.su.

Global Rights Compliance said Zhukov denied the report’s allegations, calling them “false, fabricated, and categorically rejected in their entirety”.

“The matter concerns exclusively students of a specialised college, sent to Russia within the framework of an intergovernmental agreement on the exchange of experience and the provision of venues for educational and industrial practical training,” a statement attributed to Zhukov said.

Lara Strangways, head of business and human rights at Global Rights Compliance, said the broker network pointed to deepening ties between North Korea and Russia.

“North Korean workers are being sent to Russian factories through a network that serves both states at once: Their labour props up Russian industry, including sites linked to the war in Ukraine, while the revenue they generate helps fund North Korea’s military programme,” Strangways said in a statement.

“What we are seeing is a clear exploitation of these workers as part of a cross-border system. If governments are serious about responding to this deepening alliance, they need to understand the role that forced labour is playing in sustaining it.”

North Korea and Russia have ramped up cooperation across various fields in recent years as Moscow became increasingly isolated on the international stage in the wake of its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Cold War-era allies ratified a landmark mutual defence treaty in 2024, with Pyongyang deploying thousands of North Korean soldiers to fight alongside Russian troops in the war on Ukraine.

articles.title: Google stock gets shredded after earnings—here's 2 reasons why investors hated the quarter
articles.summary: Alphabet shares get put in the penalty box after a mixed quarter.
articles.body:
Sizzling Google Cloud growth of 103% isn't going to cut it for Alphabet ( GOOGL ) bulls the day after earnings.

Alphabet shares tanked 10% in pre-market trading on Thursday after a third quarter that could best be characterized as a letdown.

The Street is locked in on two aspects of the quarter.

First, Google's search business notched sales of $63.4 billion, below the $64.9 billion expected. The miss fueled fears Google's search empire is being chipped away by the likes of Claude and ChatGPT, despite massive investment by Google.

Second, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion versus a Wall Street estimate for negative $3.5 billion. In a market getting jittery about negative free cash flow at Big Tech (see the reaction to Meta's ( META ) results last week, when it also had negative free cash flow for the first time in years), Google's print stunk up the joint.

"The bears will argue this is the first quarter that AI is starting to seriously hurt their search business and perhaps YouTube is facing some content monetization issues. Our view is that clearly there is some effect from consumers interacting with less advertising when they go to Google search and use Google AI (1B AI users and queries are at a 5 year high) as Google transitions to a world of AI and inevitably AI agents," Pivotal Research CEO Jeffrey Wlodarczak said.

Overall, Alphabet delivered a rare double-miss in its third-quarter earnings report, posting $127.57 billion in revenue against Wall Street's $128.2 billion consensus estimate.

Bottom-line results disappointed significantly as earnings per share fell to $2.12, badly missing analyst projections of $3.02 per share.

articles.summary: El economista ha reflexionado sobre el coste del mantenimiento y el descenso de inversión en el ferrocarril
articles.body: El accidente ferroviario de Urda ha conmocionado nuevamente a España. Este terrible suceso le ha costado la vida a 68 compatriotas debido a un choque por alcance de dos trenes que tenían como destino la estación de Sevilla-Santa Justa. Nuevamente, se pone en entredicho la seguridad de la red ferroviaria en España solo 9 meses después del fatídico accidente en Adamuz, que se cobró la vida de otras 46 personas. 114 muertos en un año por accidentes ferroviarios es inasumible para un país desarrollado como España, y muchas personas empiezan a señalar la falta de mantenimiento de toda la red de trenes de España. Si esto se une a que el anterior ministro de Transportes de España, que formó parte del gobierno actual, está en la cárcel por corrupción, el descontento general está justificado. En este sentido, expertos como Santiago Niño Becerra apuntan a la realidad económica española y se preguntan si realmente es asumible el gasto que se debe hacer en mantenimiento de manera anual con las vías en toda España. Para ello, el economista aporta una serie de datos como que “el mantenimiento de 1 Km de línea de AVE asciende a entre 110 y 117 m €/año”. Además, el experto explica que “si se consideran todos los servicios y amortizaciones del ciclo de explotación”, este asciende a “1,3 M €/año” y en el caso de que el mantenimiento sea de vía en túnel, “suma 1,8 M €/año”, explica en un mensaje en sus redes sociales. Finalmente, Niño Becerra hace referencia al drástico descenso de inversión pública en el transporte por ferrocarril: “pasó de 7.553,2 millones de euros en 2011 a apenas 2.214,5 millones en 2017”, parafraseando un artículo de Público donde refleja dichas cifras. Y termina con una reflexión preocupante: “¿Puede la economía de España permitirse 4.000 Km de AVE?”.

articles.title: Why Microsoft stock isn't getting crushed like Google stock after its earnings report
articles.summary: Microsoft investors aren't running for the hills after earnings. Here's the simplest reason why.
articles.body:
While Alphabet's ( GOOGL ) stock is getting crushed on Thursday after earnings, Microsoft ( MSFT ) is getting a pass.

Another way of saying it: Microsoft shares aren't trading down in sympathy.

And there is one simple reason why this is the case.

Microsoft's quarter is being seen as one of higher-than-expected growth that is sustainable, while Alphabet's quarter was sluggish and hinted at slowing growth rates in coming quarters.

Microsoft's Azure sales growth came in about 300 basis points above analyst estimates. Overall sales for the important cloud business grew 48%, excluding currency fluctuations.

Execs guided to 49% to 50% Azure sales growth in the current quarter, ahead of consensus estimates by four percentage points.

The company's capex came in about $5 billion below estimates, and other parts of the business showed sales upside.

Sales and earnings for the quarter came in ahead of analyst forecasts.

"Net/net, these results increase our confidence in the company's ability to sustain mid/upper-teens revenue growth and that strong cost of goods sold/expense operational efficiencies should be supportive of expanding operating margins," said stifel analyst Brad Reback.

Microsoft shares rose 4% in pre-market trading.

Alphabet shares tanked 10% in pre-market trading after a third quarter that could best be characterized as a letdown, both on its own and versus Microsoft.

First, Google's search business notched sales of $63.4 billion, below the $64.9 billion expected. The miss fueled fears Google's search empire is being chipped away by the likes of Claude and ChatGPT, despite massive investment by Google.

Second, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion versus a Wall Street estimate for negative $3.5 billion. In a market getting jittery about negative free cash flow at Big Tech (see the reaction to Meta's ( META ) results last week, when it also had negative free cash flow for the first time in years), Google's print stunk up the joint.

"Alphabet's 3Q results reinforced concerns we had heading into the print, re: Search is decelerating and margins have peaked near-term. This could create an air pocket over the next 1-2 quarters as investors await signs for whether this is transitory or structural," KeyBanc analyst Justin Patterson said.

articles.body: Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has asserted that the proposed India-US trade agreement will protect the sensitive interests of Indian farmers and other stakeholders, adding that its terms would put India at a strong competitive advantage once made public.Speaking at the ISID-IDRA Fourth National Conference, Goyal said Indians would welcome the agreement when its details were released.“US free trade deal, once details are out, the people of India will celebrate that not a single sensitive interest of our farmers or any stakeholder has been compromised. On October 15, Goyal said the first tranche of the proposed deal had been finalised and was undergoing legal drafting. He had expressed hope that it would be concluded soon and operationalised once India secured a competitive advantage over peer economies.Explaining the broader rationale behind India’s trade agreements, Goyal said developed countries had traditionally maintained high tariffs on labour-intensive products, creating barriers for Indian exporters. He said India had secured preferential access to markets across 38 developed and relatively prosperous countries through nine trade and bilateral agreements.“Every one of the agreement, the nine free trade deals and bilateral trade deals that we have entered into, cover 38 developed, relatively much more prosperous countries than us, and therefore they are not in competition with us...we complement each other,” he said.Goyal said the agreements had opened up preferential market access to economies with a combined gross domestic product of $60 trillion, compared with $10 trillion covered by agreements signed before 2014.“We have unlocked market opportunity at preferential rates in economies aggregating USD 60 trillion; out of these nine agreements...all the agreements prior to 2014 only covered USD 10 trillion because they were largely with countries who are in competition with us,” he added.Why India stayed out of RCEPGoyal also referred to the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), a trade bloc comprising 15 countries, including China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand and the 10 ASEAN member states.He said India was not part of the bloc when it was launched, despite being in negotiations with some of its members.“India was not in the picture at all when RCEP was launched,” he said.Goyal said India had been at an advanced stage of negotiations with Australia and could have concluded an agreement with it, while trade with New Zealand was limited at the time.“We were at an active stage of negotiation with Australia and could have finished it easily. articles.title: Alphabet and Microsoft are on both sides of the AI boom's biggest bills: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: The AI boom's biggest customers are now Big Tech's biggest bets, and the latest quarter showed which side pays off first.
articles.body:
Wall Street bought Microsoft and sold Alphabet after the two reported quarterly earnings Wednesday night. Both rent computing power to the AI labs and own stakes in them, but this quarter Microsoft cashed in while Alphabet's bets cost it.

Microsoft ( MSFT ) stock rose about 2% after hours, while Alphabet ( GOOGL , GOOG ) fell over 9%, on track for its worst day since October 2023, after its sales came up short .

For Microsoft, the labs show up as sales. OpenAI paid it $10 billion in the quarter that ended in September, according to Microsoft's quarterly filing. That's about 11% of Microsoft's $92 billion in revenue, and more than its Xbox and Windows businesses brought in combined.

Some of that money is still owed. OpenAI's unpaid bills to Microsoft rose to about $7 billion from $6 billion three months earlier. Microsoft also owns about 24% of the ChatGPT maker, but the stake barely moved its profit this time.

The order book cooled, too. Microsoft's backlog — revenue customers have signed up for, but Microsoft hasn't yet booked — slipped to about $677 billion, and new bookings fell 12% from a year earlier. CFO Amy Hood blamed "large Azure commitments in the prior year" for the tough comparison.

Alphabet's bets on the labs worked the other way. Its stakes in other companies, including roughly 14% of Anthropic and a piece of SpaceX ( SPCX ), supplied about $6 of its $9.11 in per-share profit in the second quarter.

This time they cost it. A nearly $9 billion loss on those holdings cut earnings by $0.55 a share, to $2.12. CFO Anat Ashkenazi said on the call that the loss came "primarily" from SpaceX, whose stock dropped about 12% during the quarter.

Alphabet is also footing the bill to build. It spent $51 billion on data centers and equipment in the quarter, more than double a year earlier, and burned about $9 billion in free cash flow — the cash left after those investments — for a second straight quarter. Microsoft generated about $19 billion and said it expects to stay positive this fiscal year.

To cover the gap, Alphabet bought back no stock, sold about $29 billion of bonds and $12 billion of new shares, and nearly tripled its long-term debt this year to about $125 billion. Meta ( META ) took a similar route with its nearly $100 billion stock sale .

The payoff is showing up in Google Cloud, where revenue doubled to about $31 billion and the backlog of signed contracts rose to $561 billion from $514 billion three months earlier. Anthropic has committed at least $115 billion to Google for computing power, according to its IPO filing, about a fifth of that backlog by Yahoo Finance calculations.

articles.title: Robinhood is seeing retail investor habits change dramatically as stock trading cools
articles.summary: Retail investor stock trading volume is on the decline, but investors may be simply moving to other venues, like prediction markets.
articles.body:
Retail investors are changing the way they trade.

While overall retail volumes are declining , as Goldman Sachs strategist Ben Snider wrote in a recent note, money is shifting away from traditional equities.

Instead, more investors are pouring their funds into options, leveraged ETFs, and prediction markets. Robinhood's ( HOOD ) latest earnings offer a window into the shift .

The online brokerage reported weaker-than-expected profits earlier this week as declining interest income and rising expenses weighed on the company. But it also drew record trading activity in stocks, options, and prediction markets.

Robinhood said revenue from prediction markets increased more than 500% from this time last year, up to $173 million. Customers traded a record 16.4 billion contracts during the past quarter.

Bearish sentiment has ticked up, according to a survey by Morgan Stanley Wealth Management published earlier this week. The firm found that 42% of investors are bearish this quarter, marking a 4 percentage point increase from Q3, as persistent inflation concerns, midterm election uncertainty, and rate-hike expectations prompt greater caution.

Goldman's Snider found that retail volumes have declined by about 20% since the middle of the summer and more than 40% since the end of last year. And while weaker consumer sentiment and higher energy prices partially explain the pullback, there's been a notable shift in investment vehicles.

Trading activity in leveraged ETFs has been roughly double that of ETFs tracking the same indexes without leverage, Snider's research shows. Yet another sign of appetite for riskier propositions as investors seem to be chasing the action.

And retreating from the more boring corners: Crypto's slump is also part of the changing retail investor story.

Robinhood reported that crypto trading revenue plunged 55% to $120 million amid a sharp drop-off in activity, which has broadly tracked bitcoin's 2026 fortunes.

articles.title: Employment documents every employee should preserve and why they matter
articles.summary: An appointment letter may feel important on the day an employee joins, while a salary slip may appear relevant only until the next month.
articles.body: An appointment letter may feel important on the day an employee joins, while a salary slip may appear relevant only until the next month. In reality, these records can become critical years later, when changing jobs, correcting provident fund records, filing a tax return, establishing gratuity eligibility or resolving a dispute over salary and service.Employees should therefore maintain a personal employment archive throughout their working life. It should cover not only documents received at joining and exit, but also statutory declarations, nominations and social-security records created during employment.1. Appointment letter and subsequent employment termsThe appointment letter is the starting point of the employment relationship. It ordinarily records the employee’s designation, date of joining, place of work, compensation, probation, notice period and other conditions of employment.Employees should preserve:The signed appointment or employment letterThe detailed compensation annexureDocuments confirming probation completion or employment confirmationLetters recording promotion, transfer or change in designationRevised compensation lettersAmendments to employment termsRelevant policy acknowledgementsWhy does this matter? An employee’s original terms may subsequently change several times. Preserving only the latest letter may make it difficult to establish the complete employment history.Appointment letters are also increasingly recognised as an important statutory employment record. For example, the notified Uttar Pradesh Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Rules, 2026 require an appointment letter containing prescribed particulars, including the employee code, date of joining, wages, nature of duties and applicable EPFO and ESIC benefits.2. Salary or wage slips and supporting payment recordsEvery monthly salary or wage slip should be downloaded and stored outside the employer’s portal. It usually provides a month-by-month record of basic pay, allowances, attendance or paid days, overtime, statutory contributions, tax deductions and net payment.The wage-slip requirement is not merely an HR practice. Applicable wage rules may require employers to issue wage slips electronically or otherwise on or before payment of wages.The precise format may depend on the appropriate government and the rules applicable to the establishment.Employees should periodically compare the slip with:The amount credited to their bank accountTheir agreed salary structureEPF and ESI contribution recordsTax deducted and reflected in tax recordsOvertime, incentives, bonuses and authorised deductionsA salary slip can help establish both earnings and statutory deductions. However, a bank statement shows only the amount credited; it does not explain how that amount was calculated. Both records should therefore be preserved.3. PF Form 11, UAN and provident fund recordsAn employee joining an establishment covered by the Employees’ Provident Funds framework is generally asked to complete Form 11. It captures, among other things, whether the person was previously a member of EPF or EPS and, where applicable, the existing Universal Account Number, previous PF account details and KYC information.Employees should retain:A copy or acknowledgement of Form 11Their UAN and member IDs linked to itUAN activation details, without sharing or recording passwords insecurelyAadhaar, PAN and bank-account linkage statusAnnual or periodic EPF passbooksTransfer-claim acknowledgementsJoint declarations or correction requestsScheme certificates or pension-related records, where applicableClaim applications and settlement communicationsThe official EPFO portal provides access to the member passbook and claim status. EPFO also permits members to file and update electronic nominations during service.Employees should review their EPF passbook after joining a new employer and periodically thereafter. A mismatch in name, date of birth, date of joining, date of exit or previous employment details may otherwise remain unnoticed.Importantly, an EPF nomination is separate from a gratuity nomination. Updating one should not be assumed to update the other.4. ESI insurance number, e-Pehchan card and family detailsEmployees covered under the Employees’ State Insurance Scheme should preserve their insurace or IP number, e-Pehchan card and the registration particulars of eligible family members.The e-Pehchan framework supports identification of the insured person and registered family members for access to services.Relevant records include:Temporary identity certificate, where issuedESI insurance or IP numbere-Pehchan cardUpdated family particularsMedical or benefit-related certificatesClaim applications, approvals and payment recordsAccident or employment-injury documents, where relevantEmployees should not rely exclusively on continuing access to the employer’s HR portal after separation.5. Form 16 and annual tax recordsForm 16 is an important annual tax document for a salaried employee. Employees should preserve Form 16 issued by every employer during a financial year, particularly if they change jobs.They should also retain:Form 12BB and supporting declarations submitted to the employerProof of tax-saving investments and eligible deductionsRent receipts and landlord particulars submitted for HRA purposesForm 26AS and Annual Information StatementFiled income-tax returns and acknowledgementsTax-demand, refund or rectification communicationsThe Income Tax Department maintains a dedicated Form 16 resource and separate guidance for returns applicable to salaried individuals.Form 16 should not be viewed as an infallible record. Employees should reconcile salary and TDS information with Form 26AS and the Annual Information Statement before filing their return.6. Statutory nomination formsNomination forms often receive less attention than salary documents, although their importance is greatest when an employee is not available to clarify their wishes.Employees should preserve acknowledged copies of all applicable nominations, including:EPF and EPS nominationGratuity nominationESI family or dependant particularsEmployer group life and accident insurance nominationsSuperannuation or pension-fund nominationNPS nomination, where applicableWage, maternity-benefit or other statutory nomination forms prescribed under the applicable rulesUnder the Social Security (Central) Rules, 2026 , Form III is the prescribed nomination form. The same form will be used for a fresh nomination and modification of an existing nomination.A nomination should be reviewed following marriage, divorce, birth or adoption of a child, death of a nominee or any significant change in family circumstances. Employees should obtain an employer acknowledgement or retain the electronic confirmation. A form that was submitted but cannot later be traced may create avoidable difficulty.7. Leave, maternity and workplace-benefit recordsEmployees should retain significant leave and benefit records, particularly where they affect continuity of service or payment. These may include:Maternity leave application and approvalMedical certificates and fitness documentsAdoption, commissioning-mother or childcare-related approvals, where applicableLong-service, sabbatical or unpaid-leave approvalsEmployment-injury and disability-related recordsApproved work-from-home or remote-working arrangements where these change employment conditionsSensitive medical records should be stored securely and shared only where required.8. Resignation, acceptance and exit documentsAn employee should preserve both the resignation submitted and the employer’s response. A verbal resignation or an unrecorded discussion may not satisfactorily establish the agreed last working day.The exit file should include:Resignation email or signed letterEmployer’s acceptanceAgreed last working dayNotice-period waiver, recovery or buyout communicationHandover and no-dues acknowledgementsRelieving letterService certificate or experience letterFull-and-final settlement statementGratuity calculation and payment communication, where applicableLeave-encashment and bonus detailsFinal salary slip and bank-credit proofPF exit-date and transfer recordsA service certificate, experience letter and relieving letter may serve different purposes. The service or experience document generally records the period and nature of employment, while the relieving letter confirms that the employee has been released from service.Employees should check that the dates, designation and employer’s legal name are accurate.Practical exampleRiya changes employment after seven years. Four years later, she finds that her date of exit from the earlier employment was incorrectly recorded in her PF account. Her old HR portal is no longer accessible.Because she retained her appointment letter, salary slips, resignation acceptance, relieving letter, PF member details and full-and-final settlement, she has a coherent record of when her employment began and ended. Without these documents, resolving the discrepancy could be considerably harder.Build one secure employment archiveEmployees should create separate folders for each employer and organise records under joining, payroll, tax, social security, nominations, benefits and exit. Important documents should be downloaded before the last working day and retained in a secure personal location, with an encrypted backup.The practical rule is simple: preserve any document that establishes who employed you, on what terms, for what period, how much you were paid, what statutory deductions were made, which benefits covered you and who was nominated to receive them. A few minutes spent maintaining these records can protect years of employment, tax and social-security history.Employee document health checkAt least once a year, employees should verify:Are all appointment, increment and promotion letters available?Have salary slips and Form 16 been downloaded?Do salary deductions reconcile with EPF, ESI and tax records?Are UAN, KYC, bank and family details correct?Are all benefit nominations current and acknowledged?Are records from previous employers still accessible?Are employment documents stored securely outside the employer’s systems?Following an exit, have the service certificate, final settlement and statutory benefit records been collected?A well-maintained employment archive is not paperwork for its own sake. It is a personal record of an employee’s earnings, service, rights and financial security.(The author, Puneet Gupta is Partner, People Advisory Services Tax at EY India)You use AI every day. articles.title: Samsung Electronics Shares Slide After Return Plan Is Delayed
articles.summary: Samsung Electronics Co. shares reversed earlier gains to slide as much as 6.6% as the lack of a new shareholder return plan in its earnings disappointed inve...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Samsung Electronics Co. ( 005930.KS ) shares reversed earlier gains to slide as much as 6.6% as the lack of a new shareholder return plan in its earnings disappointed investors.

The Korean chipmaker said it will announce the plan at the end of January, a contrast with its peer SK Hynix Inc. that delivered a blockbuster earnings report Wednesday along with its intention to return about $45 billion more to shareholders. Sentiment toward Samsung was also hurt as profit from the company's chip operations missed estimates and capital expenditure expanded.

"Making the market wait until January for the full return plan has left a hole right where the good news should have been," said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at eToro. "Samsung is also lifting capex by around 60% this year, so until it spells out how this windfall gets split between new capacity and shareholders, there's a genuine question mark over how much actually comes back to investors."

Samsung said in August it planned to return as much as 110 trillion won ($82.5 billion) to investors this year.

"Deferring the shareholder return details to January is disappointing," said Rob Li, managing partner at New York-based Amont Partners. "This gives excuses to stock traders to rotate money to SK Hynix or Micron in the next few months as the other two have a clearer shareholder return path."

South Korea's Kospi index fell as much as 3.2% after surging 6.6% on Thursday. SK Hynix pared its earlier gains of 6.7% to be up by 1.8%.

articles.title: DoorDash to acquire Instacart for $17 billion, creating delivery giant
articles.summary: Delivery giant DoorDash is buying to-your-door grocery service Instacart for $17 billion, the company announced Thursday.
articles.body: Delivery giant DoorDash is buying to-your-door grocery service Instacart for $17 billion, the company announced Thursday. The deal means users will be able to order groceries and items from other retailers via DoorDash and its delivery network. The companies said Instacart customers can now shop at more than 50,000 additional stores on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today. DashPass and Instacart+ members will now also pay one membership fee instead of two. DoorDash is expected to keep the Instacart brand and its technology. Until the transaction closes, DoorDash and Instacart will continue to operate as separate and independent companies. “Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more,” Instacart CEO Chris Rogers said. DoorDash shares gained more than 9% in pre-market trading Thursday. The deal represents the latest chapter of consolidation in the delivery industry. Last year, DoorDash bought United Kingdom-based Deliveroo, while Uber now owns Postmates ​and Delivery Hero. DoorDash has emerged as the most successful stand-alone online delivery platform in America, commanding some two-thirds of all food delivery volumes as of 2024, according to Bloomberg data. But over the past year, the company has seen its share price decline by approximately a third, largely due to rising costs. Instacart, meanwhile, reached the pinnacle of its success during the Covid pandemic, when lockdowns sent millions of consumers to their phones to order grocery deliveries. But the company’s stock has gone nowhere over the past two years, as Instacart struggled to find new paths to growth while facing increasing competition from Amazon and Walmart’s grocery delivery offerings. While a merger would create cost savings by allowing the combined company to reduce its corporate workforce and split some expenses, it’s not clear how much more money there remains that can be squeezed out of delivery customers. Americans who eat at home have begun to complain about the price of food delivery — and the pinch has only worsened this year amid soaring fuel costs, which have led to new fees and surcharges. A recent debate about the cost of having a burrito delivered went viral, as social media users argued over whether $20 was a reasonable price to pay to have the Tex-Mex treat delivered. Platforms such as DoorDash and Instacart have also faced legal scrutiny over how they treat those who make deliveries for their respective platforms. Last month, DoorDash settled with New York City regulators for $131.5 million to resolve charges it deprived workers of millions of dollars in tips. “Simply put, we screwed up,” the San ‌Francisco-based ⁠company said in a statement. “Our mistakes meant some Dashers were underpaid or paid late. While these mistakes weren’t intentional, that doesn’t make them okay.” The proposed transaction was first reported by tech website The Information and The Wall Street Journal.

articles.title: DoorDash acquires Instacart for $17 billion, doubling down on hyper-local delivery
articles.summary: It's official, two of the largest third-party delivery apps, are coming together.
articles.body:
DoorDash ( DASH ) announced plans to acquire hyper-local grocery delivery provider Instacart ( CART ) on Thursday morning in a deal valued at $17 billion.

DoorDash, which is primarily known for its restaurant food delivery business, will pay $65 per Instacart share, a 26% premium over the stock's Oct. 22 closing price. The transaction includes 75% cash, with Instacart stockholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock, or a combination of both. Instacart's board of directors unanimously approved the deal, according to a press release.

"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online," DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in the release. "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery."

DoorDash stock popped over 5% in premarket trading, while Instacart stock edged lower.

The acquisition comes as Walmart ( WMT ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) have been taking share of the grocery delivery market, especially for same-day and one-hour delivery.

Prior to the announcement, Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian said the combination of Instacart and DoorDash could "potentially prove to be a competitive differentiation."

"A combination of strong restaurant delivery plus a marketplace including various grocers from Instacart can be a critical combination against Walmart and Amazon in particular, who continue to push in this market as well," Arounian said.

Walmart currently holds roughly a 30.9% share of online grocery, ahead of Amazon at roughly 23.6%, per Wedbush.

For customers worried about what the Instacart acquisition means for prices, the company said shoppers will now get two memberships for the price of one and more choices.

"Instacart customers could shop at more than 50,000 additional stores, on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today," the release said.

For local business owners, the company said this would allow them more ways to earn.

articles.title: DoorDash strikes $17 billion deal for US rival Instacart in bets on grocery delivery
articles.summary: Oct 29 (Reuters) - DoorDash said on Thursday it would buy Instacart in a deal valued at about $17 billion, stepping up its push into the fast-growing US groc...
articles.body:
Oct 29 (Reuters) - DoorDash said on Thursday it would buy Instacart in a deal valued at about $17 billion, stepping up its push into the ‌fast-growing US grocery delivery market as competition among app-based platforms intensifies.

Heightened competition ‌following a slowdown in orders from pandemic-era peaks, along with rising costs and tougher regulatory scrutiny over ​the treatment of gig workers, has spurred a wave of dealmaking across the industry.

Meanwhile, delivery companies chasing growth are expanding into grocery, convenience and other retail categories as their core food-delivery businesses mature.

"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online," ‌said Tony Xu, co-founder and ⁠CEO of DoorDash, adding Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers.

Online grocery delivery has also gained traction as ⁠consumers increasingly prize convenience, while a recent surge in gasoline prices linked to disruptions from the war in Iran could give shoppers another reason to avoid trips to stores.

DoorDash ​has offered ​Instacart shareholders $65 per share held, representing a ​premium of about 26% to the ‌stock's closing price on October 22 before reports of deal talks first emerged.

The consideration will be at least 75% cash, with Instacart shareholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock or a combination of the two, the companies said.

Shares of Instacart, formally known as Maplebear, were flat at $58.50 in premarket trading. They had hit a record high ‌of $62 on Monday.

DoorDash shares jumped nearly 7% ​after the company also reported better-than-expected quarterly revenue. They ​have declined about 25% so ​far this year through their last close.

The transaction is expected to ‌close at the end of 2027 or ​the first half ​of 2028.

The deal could face scrutiny over its impact on competition, with New York City's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) saying on Wednesday that a ​potential merger continued a "troubling ‌trend" of corporate consolidation.

DoorDash, however, pledged on Thursday that local grocers could ​continue to work with any delivery platform they choose.

(Reporting by Anuja Bharat ​Mistry in Bengaluru; Editing by Sriraj Kalluvila)

articles.title: US GDP accelerates to 3.4% in the third quarter
articles.summary: Gross domestic product increased at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter.
articles.body:
The US economy grew at a robust pace in the third quarter, driven by investment, consumer spending, and government spending.

Gross domestic product increased at a 3.4% annualized rat e, according to an initial estimate released Thursday by the US Bureau of Economic Analysis, beating economists' expectations of 3.1% and marking an acceleration from the second quarter's 2.2% growth.

Third-quarter growth was partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are subtracted in the calculation of GDP, increased. The artificial intelligence build-out was the main engine, with business investment surging 12.7%. Consumer spending grew 3.8%, matching the rate in Q2 and the strongest since the end of 2024.

The release is the final report on the economy ahead of next week's midterm elections, in which economic and cost-of-living issues are front and center.

Molly Moorhead is economics editor at Yahoo Finance.

articles.title: PCE inflation shows prices ticked higher in September, keeping expectations for a year-end hike
articles.summary: The Personal Consumption Expenditures index rose 3.6%, in line with expectations and up from 3.4% a month earlier.
articles.body:
A fresh reading of the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge showed prices heated up in September, solidifying expectations for an interest rate hike in December.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures index rose 3.6%, in line with expectations and up from 3.4% a month earlier. On a core basis, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, PCE rose 3.1%, also in line with expectations and up a tenth of a percentage point from 3% in August. Month over month, core PCE clocked in at 0.3%, in line with projections, marking a faster pace from the 0.2% seen in August.

The data was anticipated, prompting many analysts to feel a rate hike was in order Wednesday, given other inflation readings ahead of the Fed's meeting that showed price increases last month.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh provided no intricate explanation Wednesday of why the central bank chose to hold rates steady after a hot reading on the Consumer Price Index and ahead of core PCE that was expected to show prices moving up at a faster pace than in August, the catalyst for September's hike.

Markets are pricing in a better than 80% chance that the central bank hikes rates in December.

While Warsh didn't send an explicit signal that the Fed would hike at its next meeting, he did say that since September, credit conditions have tightened for some businesses and households but still aren't tight, implying there's still room for the central bank to raise rates further.

articles.title: DoorDash buying Instacart for $17B
articles.summary: DoorDash announced Thursday it will acquire Instacart, buying the grocery delivery company for around $17 billion. Instacart will keep its brand name, and customers will be able to continue using the app for their grocery shopping orders, DoorDash said in a statement. The acquisition received unanimous approval from Instacart’s board of directors. The deal will…
articles.body:
DoorDash announced Thursday it will acquire Instacart, buying the grocery delivery company for around $17 billion.

Instacart will keep its brand name, and customers will be able to continue using the app for their grocery shopping orders, DoorDash said in a statement . The acquisition received unanimous approval from Instacart’s board of directors.

The deal will allow for Instacart users to shop at an additional 50,000 stores on top of the nearly 100,000 stores already accessible through its platform, according to DoorDash. DashPass and Instacart+ memberships will merge together, but shoppers will only have to pay the price of one.

Instacart CEO Chris Rogers said the company “has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more.”

“Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve,” he said in DoorDash’s statement.

Both companies run on independent contractors collecting and delivering preselected grocery shopping orders, with access to various grocery and convenience store chains. DoorDash’s partnerships with stores expanded last year after agreeing to list Kroger’s full inventory of 2,700 U.S. stores, as well as last month after agreeing to deliver products from Costco.

“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online,” DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in the statement. “Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”

DoorDash expanded to delivering groceries in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic after serving as a restaurant order-delivery business. It completed 3 billion orders in 2025, with 9 million independent workers carrying out deliveries.

Last month, it agreed to pay $115 million to 260,000-plus workers it either did not pay at all or paid late as part of a settlement with New York City’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection. The settlement was in connection with claims that DoorDash underpaid its workers.

DoorDash acknowledged that it “screwed up” while it denied that payment errors were intentional.

articles.title: Is Fox News pivoting to its post-Trump era? Look at how it’s covering the midterms
articles.summary: President Trump is “dominating the airwaves and controlling the conversation,” Fox host Jesse Watters declared on October 21, touting the president’s midterm blitz. Trump was speaking in South Carolina at that same moment. Fox didn’t carry any of it live.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is “dominating the airwaves and controlling the conversation,” Fox News host Jesse Watters declared on October 21, touting the president’s midterm campaign blitz. Trump was speaking in South Carolina at that same moment. Fox didn’t carry any of it live. As Republicans fight to retain control of Congress, the party’s most powerful television ally has been making its own choices about what the closing message should be — cheering Trump’s campaigning while frequently avoiding his speeches. The Murdochs are thinking about a post-Trump era and looking ahead to the 2028 presidential election — believing the network will be center stage as both the Republicans and Democrats choose nominees. But right now, Fox’s ratings are down, and its defenses are up. The country’s dominant conservative network is a reflection of Republican malaise amid a midterm season that has given the party little to cheer about. Several of its hosts sound not just determined, but downright desperate to juice GOP turnout. Some Trump fans have literally tuned it all out. Normally cable news ratings surge during an election season, but Fox’s total audience fell about 27% in October compared with the same month a year ago. The Hollywood Reporter called it the steepest decline suffered by any cable news network in the run-up to an election in the past decade. The Bulwark’s culture editor Sonny Bunch said in response, “This is probably more revealing of GOP enthusiasm than every poll released thus far.” Fox still commands a huge audience, however, including many voters who identify as independents and liberals. That’s partly why Democrats like Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed have popped up on Fox’s air in recent weeks, courting voters who are disappointed by Trump and willing to consider a Democrat. Trump, in turn, has railed against Fox when he has seen Democrats on the network that he considers his own. Right now Fox’s profitable but difficult alliance with Trump is being tested like never before. Fox’s fading appetite for Trump The change in Fox’s appetite for Trump’s speeches is striking. From January through September, Trump delivered 14 campaign-style rally speeches, and Fox News took 12 of them live, a CNN analysis finds. In fact, the network was so eager to show the president speaking that when Trump briefly handed the microphone to a few members of Congress during a July 27 rally in Michigan, host Brian Kilmeade assured viewers that Fox’s cutaway would be brief. “We’ll bring you back there live when he starts speaking again,” he said, “and we won’t have you miss any of the action.” During Trump’s fall midterm blitz, however, Fox viewers have missed a lot of Trump action, so to speak. The network aired live portions of just nine of his 24 speeches, according to CNN’s tally through Wednesday night. In early October, Fox routinely ignored Trump’s live events and showed only short clips of the speeches afterward. This approach continued until late in the month, when Fox began to dip into the president’s speeches with some regularity. The bulk of the rally airtime has been during the network’s weekend programming, which is lower-rated than weekday commentary shows like “The Five” and “Jesse Watters Primetime.” Fox has appeared loath to interrupt its most popular shows for Trump, particularly when he is just repeating his stump speech. (Fox has live-streamed every rally online.) Even Newsmax, Fox’s far-less-popular rival for MAGA viewership, has dialed back on airing Trump’s rallies compared with earlier this year, often airing just a few minutes before directing viewers to its paid app for the rest, CNN analysis found. “I hate to do this. I hate interrupting the president,” Newsmax host Greg Kelly said while cutting away from Trump’s October 1 rally after about three minutes. He promised to watch the rest later — “You always learn things” — but explained: “We have some other content that we have to get through.” The slow backing away from Trump’s rallies comes as he registers some of the weakest approval ratings of his presidency and seeks to preserve Republican congressional majorities that are threatened in part by his own unpopularity. (Earlier this month, Fox’s own polling unit put Trump’s job approval at 36%, a record low in the network’s polling.) Trump’s long, meandering speeches ostensibly promote GOP candidates, but can veer into extended airings of personal grievances, sales pitches for expensive White House renovations and all-too-frequent observations about the male physique. Meanwhile, Fox’s hosts can offer a more focused Republican pitch, and that’s exactly what they do. Hour after hour, hosts and guests decry the Democratic Party and denounce socialism. In recent days, they have stoked fear about riots in France spreading stateside and summoned outrage over Barack Obama’s supposed snobbery toward the Cheesecake Factory. Watters remarked earlier this month that “fear porn” is necessary to motivate voters: “You have to say ‘These people will take your health care. They’re going to let in the third world. They’re going to jack up your taxes.’ And that’s what’s going to get people to come out to vote. You have to say, ‘These people are scary and dangerous. You know what we’re all about.’ And that’s really a choice.” On Wednesday night, though, Watters let Trump do most of the talking. The president’s Ohio speech ran uninterrupted for almost the entire hour. The ratings warning sign From a business standpoint, Fox News is the envy of the cable television universe. The network commands a large and loyal audience and ranks as the top-rated channel across all of cable in prime time, easily outrating CNN and MS NOW. But Fox’s ratings have sagged sharply this fall. Some might see it as a bit of political foreshadowing. If next week is an electoral earthquake, Fox’s ratings are a foreshock, signaling what may be coming. October was Fox’s lowest-rated month since December 2023. The year-over-year audience decline suggests that “conservatives are tuning out ahead of the high-stakes elections,” as Oliver Darcy wrote for Status earlier this week. Nielsen’s recent methodology changes may also explain the decline, though CNN and MS NOW posted year-over-year gains in October, likely driven by election-season interest. Fox is used to seeing viewer mood swings show up in the ratings. In 2020, when Trump allies attacked Fox for accurately reporting that he had lost to Joe Biden, Fox’s ratings dropped precipitously. The ratings pressure was on the minds of some Fox hosts and producers who subsequently platformed Trump’s election lies, leading to multiple defamation lawsuits. That 2020 ratings decline was an election aftershock. The Fox base slowly but surely tuned back in over time. But at the moment, Trump fatigue is taking a real toll on Fox’s ratings, and thus its bottom line. ‘Why are they doing this???’ Some Democrats running in red and purple states have seen Fox as a useful platform to campaign. David Jolly, the Democratic candidate for governor in Florida, gave an interview to Fox’s Bill Hemmer and Dana Perino earlier this week, recognizing the network’s large audience across the state. Jolly shared the interview on social media afterward and thanked the hosts for the invitation. El-Sayed and Kentucky Senate Democratic candidate Charles Booker have also appeared on the network recently. But for every Democrat who has said yes to a Fox interview, many have said no, reflecting the party’s split over whether to treat the network as an opponent or an opportunity. Trump and some of his aides have bristled at El-Sayed’s visibility on Fox. The president railed against host Martha MacCallum’s “softball” interview with El-Sayed earlier this month. Then he attacked Fox for giving airtime to the independent candidate challenging Nebraska’s Republican Senate incumbent. “Fox News is long form interviewing the sleazebag, Dan Osborn, right now, who is running against our GREAT Republican Senator, Pete Ricketts, from Nebraska,” the president wrote. “Why are they doing this???” The network rarely talks about its coverage choices and avoids responding to the president’s missives. But Fox News president Jay Wallace, during an unrelated interview with Axios, alluded to Trump’s anger about El-Sayed and said, “Someone didn’t necessarily like that. But that’s what we do.” Wallace’s rebuttal is obvious: Fox’s news programs are supposed to cover all the news, not just GOP views, even though the network is largely defined by pro-Trump opinion shows that repeat the GOP party line. Even those opinion shows can contain surprising moments. A new El-Sayed campaign ad features Watters and other Fox figures making flattering remarks about the Democratic candidate and skeptical remarks about Mike Rogers, the Trump-backed Republican in the race. Meanwhile, Trump remains dependent on Fox to reach the voter base he shares with the network. The relationship is likely to remain awkward. Trump has signaled that he might scapegoat Fox for Republican losses next week. “Fox News is spending far too much time putting on the OPPONENTS of Republican party candidates,” he complained over the weekend. Trump claimed that Fox’s lack of “help” is “the only reason this race is close, if it is indeed close.”

articles.title: As US midterms approach, farmers decide what to plant and how to vote
articles.summary: In Arkansas, rising costs spurred farmer Hallie Shoffner’s long-shot Senate campaign. Will farmers back her?
articles.body:
When Paul McKinney, a farmer in northeast Arkansas, thinks of his son’s childhood, he remembers a small boy playing in vast fields.

To a child, a flooded rice field is “like a giant, 40-acre swimming pool”, he said.

Rice has been a staple on McKinney’s farm for four generations. Next year, however, the family plans to plant much less. Instead, they will focus on soya, a crop that is cheaper to produce.

Like farmers across the United States , McKinney is making tough decisions this year in response to higher fuel and fertiliser costs, which have skyrocketed since the start of the war on Iran.

This week, farmers also face tough choices at the polls. Democrats are expected to make gains in the midterm elections, as voters react to high prices economy-wide by switching parties or staying home.

Observers are watching farm country closely. Texas and Kansas could send Democrats to the Senate for the first time in decades. In the House of Representatives, two majority-rural districts, Wisconsin’s Third and North Carolina First, could become tipping points for Democratic control.

Still, many of the country’s most rural areas, like Arkansas, are also its most safely Republican.

That leaves an uphill battle for Democrat Hallie Shoffner, who quit farming last year to challenge Republican Senator Tom Cotton in a campaign squarely focused on rising costs.

Even before the US-Israel war on Iran, high input costs were straining farmers, said Ryan Loy, an extension economist for the University of Arkansas’ Division of Agriculture.

Loy pointed to a trade war with China that began in 2018, the ongoing war in Ukraine and disruptions related to the 2025 tariffs as factors driving up input costs and disrupting markets. A drought across the US heartland, made worse by climate change, has added to the strain.

Farmers across the country are working to adapt. In Arkansas, many farmers skipped rice in favour of soya. Soya is “the least input-intensive crop, and perhaps can break even or have the shallowest loss”, Loy said.

Now Arkansas, usually the country’s top rice producer, has its lowest rice acreage since the 1970s. Many farmers hoped 2026 would bring economic recovery so they could return to rice.

Then, the war on Iran hit. With the Strait of Hormuz blocked, fertiliser costs jumped just as farmers were fertilising during the spring planting season.

Loy tracked the increase in a sample budget that he maintains for Arkansas row crop farmers. “Urea fertiliser specifically peaked about 39 percent over our budgeted amount,” Loy said. Diesel costs came in about 72 percent more than budget averaged across the planting, growing and harvesting seasons, Loy found.

Those changes represent a significant economic hit. “For our state alone, it’s an additional cost of about $343m,” Loy said.

Last week, US President Donald Trump announced an $8bn fuel relief programme for farmers, following $12bn in tariff-related aid in 2025. If the fuel relief payment were divided equally between the 50 states, it would cover less than half of the extra costs that Loy estimates Arkansas’ farmers paid this year.

McKinney, a member of the Arkansas Farm Bureau, said the announcement was welcome. Still, he hoped for longer-term solutions that would prevent “this constant battle for survival”.

For many farms, survival is indeed getting harder. Farm bankruptcies for the first three quarters of 2026 were up 19 percent compared to this time last year, according to a recent analysis by the University of Arkansas’ National Agricultural Law Center. They were up 73 percent compared to 2024.

McKinney’s son, who grew up playing in muddy rice fields, now helps his dad farm their 24,000 acres. So does McKinney’s nephew, who this year is driving a combine.

“As has been done for us, we would love to be able to hand that down to the next generation,” said McKinney. “But you also have to think about what is going to be best for them.”

McKinney questions how long farming will provide a sustainable living. “It’s some heavy things to think about,” McKinney said.

For Shoffner, a sixth-generation Arkansas farmer, that reckoning came last year.

Higher costs, lower crop prices and the uncertainty of trade wars and tariffs “made the numbers stop working” for their 2,000-acre farm operation, Shoffner told Al Jazeera.

“I know what it feels like to work hard, make every adjustment you can, and still have to sit down with your family and say, ‘We can’t keep doing this,’” Shoffner said.

To protect her parents’ land and retirement, Shoffner closed the family’s farm. That “heartbreaking” decision helped spur her Senate run.

“I decided that if I can’t farm, I will fight,” Shoffner said.

If elected, Shoffner wants to end the war on Iran, build trade policies farmers “can actually plan around”, invest in local processing and distribution, and pass a robust Farm Bill — strategies she hopes will help farmers and rural economies more broadly.

“If we want rural communities to have a future, the people producing our food have to be able to make a living doing it.”

Cotton did not respond to a request for comment.

Economic pain may not change farmers’ votes, however, in Arkansas or nationwide. Michael Shepherd, a political scientist at the University of Michigan, said many farmers, like many rural voters, are committed Republicans.

Committed voters tend to view the economy through a partisan lens, according to Shepherd. “Their political behaviours, their voting choices, things like that, are not particularly responsive to changes in the agricultural economy,” he said.

Some polling this year, however, did suggest the potential for movement. A poll by the Farm Journal in April found that 35 percent of farmers who “usually” vote Republican and 15 percent who “always” vote Republican were still considering how they would vote.

And September polling from Purdue showed that, for the first time this term, a majority of farmers surveyed think the country is “on the wrong track”.

Even if farmers are swayable, of course, Shoffner still may not be the one to sway them: her campaign has been far outspent by Cotton’s, an established lawmaker who has received funding from interest groups like AIPAC and leaders at companies like Anthropic and Palantir.

“If one side has a massive war chest, and the other side has very limited resources, then that game of tug of war can be won much easier than it should be,” Shepherd said.

And even if farmers do change their votes, they may not decide elections.

McKinney, who is now farming one of the Shoffner family’s former fields, said farmers represent a shrinking percentage of rural voters — their strength now is in organising, not numbers.

Still, even where candidates like Shoffner don’t win, their campaigns might signal to funders that similar races may be competitive in the future or help Democrats win down-ballot seats.

In Arkansas’ second congressional district, for example, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is betting on Democrat Chris Jones. It’s a long-shot campaign, but across the country, at least some long-shot candidates are expected to win.

“All indications are that this is gonna be one of the biggest shifts away from the president’s party that we’ve observed,” Shepherd said.

articles.title: AI founders want to give shares to the public? Give them to Social Security.
articles.summary: Congress should build an independent fund that accepts contributed equity from any company, holds it in a diversified portfolio and dedicates the returns to the trust funds.
articles.body:
Anthropic, readying an initial public offering that investors reportedly value at $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion said it will commit 5 percent of its shares, subject to shareholder approval, to a new Public Benefit Fund, with up to 2 percent more for every 50 percent gain in the company’s value. With earlier pledges, roughly a fifth of the company is earmarked for the public good.

Elon Musk’s response : Give the shares directly to the public. On Oct. 19, he pledged to do it himself: one SpaceX share, currently worth about $146, to every American child next year.

He is closer to right than he knows. The country already has an institution that insures nearly every worker against lost earnings and pays those workers directly: Social Security. But Social Security is not allowed to own equity shares; by law it may hold only federal debt .

Congress should build an independent fund that accepts contributed equity from any company, holds it in a diversified portfolio and dedicates the returns to the trust funds. Canada’s pension plan, Norway’s oil fund, Alaska’s Permanent Fund and state pension systems own equity on the public’s behalf. To allay any fears, the fund’s governance should be boring by design, with no government board seats, no political direction and a published schedule for selling each stock down into a broad index.

Anthropic and Musk are not alone in wanting the public to share in AI’s gains. OpenAI’s April policy paper proposed a public wealth fund investing in AI companies and paying returns to citizens. In July, the Financial Times reported Sam Altman had offered 5 percent of the company’s equity to seed a sovereign wealth fund. Politicians from President Trump to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) have called for public investment funds.

None of these has produced a working fund. Social Security, by contrast, is up and running. It covers nearly every American worker and ended last year with $2.6 trillion in reserves, all in special-issue Treasuries. But it is underpowered and shrinking. The Trustees project the retirement trust fund will run out in late 2032, when benefits would be cut 22 percent.

To be clear, AI equity pledges alone are not a sufficient funding fix. Anthropic’s 5 percent is worth $75 billion to $100 billion, and OpenAI’s offer about $60 billion, at reported valuations. The program’s 75-year shortfall is $29 trillion in present value .

But equities belong in Social Security’s portfolio, as in any retirement account. A diversified fund earning 2.5 to 3 points a year over Treasuries ( within the range Social Security’s own actuaries assume ), with returns reinvested, could turn every $100 billion contributed today into $600 billion to nearly $900 billion in present value over the Trustees’ window.

Sens. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) and Tim Kaine (D-Va.) have a plan to borrow $1.5 trillion to seed a Social Security investment fund . We share their aim of higher returns, but borrowing creates financing risks. The debt comes due whatever markets do, and the new borrowing would pile onto a growing federal debt just as long-term Treasury yields have hit their highest level since 2002 .

Contribute the money instead, and those financing risks disappear. The same sum could close a third to nearly half the gap, shrinking the tax increases and benefit cuts otherwise needed.

AI shares should be the catalyst for larger funding sources, starting with existing federal assets. Treasury holds a senior stake in Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac that J.P. Morgan estimates will reach roughly $400 billion by year-end, plus warrants for nearly 80 percent of their common shares. Officials have proposed selling slivers while keeping the companies in conservatorship. The government’s 261 million ounces of gold are worth about $1.1 trillion at recent prices and earn no yield.

Together that is about $1.5 trillion, what Cassidy and Kaine want to borrow, before counting a single AI share or warrant.

Washington already allows donated corporate stock in a federal program. Last year Congress created Trump Accounts for children and Treasury now lets companies and charities donate public stock into them. If a child’s account can hold donated stock, so should the program that pays 71 million Americans today and nearly all the rest of us when we retire.

The companies’ offer can be made conditional on Congress acting, a long-standing tactic in American philanthropy. Andrew Carnegie paid for nearly 1,700 public library buildings, but only in towns that supplied the land and committed public money to run them. Here, it would give Congress something to say yes to: neither a tax increase nor a benefit cut.

Anthropic says it will share more about its fund’s governance in the coming months. The company can commit now to contributing if Congress builds the vehicle. Congress can build it as part of any solvency deal, or on its own.

Social Security was the institutional answer to a great economic dislocation. The companies most confident that another is coming have begun, voluntarily, to put equity on the table. The public should have an account to receive it. The first companies to contribute will have done for this century what Carnegie did for the public library.

Eftychis Gregos-Mourginakis is co-founder of Kibu, Inc. Jan Jaro is an investor at Helena and an advisor at the Federation of American Scientists.

articles.title: Hershey CEO offers a ghoulish warning on how Halloween candy sales are going
articles.summary: Hershey CEO offers a measured tone on how the crucial Halloween candy season is going.
articles.body:
Hershey ( HSY ) investors were not saved by a friendly earnings day on Thursday.

Shares are melting in early trading as the chocolate giant lowered its organic sales outlook for the year to about 3%, the low end of its previous 3% to 3.5% range.

Organic sales in the third quarter grew a meager 0.8%.

Hershey shares were down 10% year to date ahead of the company's latest earnings report.

The more cautious outlook seems to stem from weakness in the all-important Halloween candy selling season, in large part because of price increases.

"Halloween participation is expected to be in line with 2025, though financial pressures could shape final purchase decisions. As expected, the compressed calendar is affecting the season's pace," Hershey CEO Kirk Tanner said on the earnings call.

He added, "We are optimistic that our enhanced assortment, new pack types and value price points, seasonal innovation, and increased investment will drive engagement in these final days leading into this weekend's celebrations. Consistent with our expectations, our actions are delivering healthy consumption trends on both a one-year and two-year basis."

Halloween candy sales declined 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared to the same period last year, according to data from NielsenIQ. The AP first reported the decline.

The data also showed an 11.7% decline in candy sales in mid-September.
