articles.title: The dangerous financial web behind the surging AI bubble
articles.summary: Silicon Valley’s unregulated bank must be brought to heel.
articles.body:
Much has been said about the shaky financing of the current AI wave: the pool of money is huge, the bets are risky, and U.S. economic growth hinges on the market’s continued expansion. This past month has brought these issues into stark relief, with CoreWeave’s stock plummeting amid its mounting debt burden and fears of an AI bubble.

But the corporation escaping scrutiny in all this is Nvidia, whose monopoly over chip design and vast amounts of capital have allowed it to shape the AI capital market to its own ends, furthering its dominance of AI infrastructure and destabilizing the U.S. economy as it proceeds unchecked.

Nvidia was founded in 1993 as a small startup optimizing semiconductor chips for gamers who needed more computing power to render graphics quickly. But things started to change in the early 2010s with the rapid surge of interest in developing artificial intelligence. AI models required a large amount of specialized computational power, and Nvidia’s graphics processing units were ideally suited to AI use cases.

This marked a turning point for Nvidia. In 2016, co-founder and president Jensen Huang personally gifted an Nvidia supercomputer to OpenAI, recently founded by Elon Musk, Sam Altman and others, virtually guaranteeing that OpenAI’s software would primarily use Nvidia chips. Nvidia also began courting scientists and AI researchers by donating its processing units and supercomputers. By 2023, Nvidia’s stock price had begun a steep upward climb that culminated, by mid-2025, in the company being named the most valuable public company in the world.

Once the AI world started running on Nvidia graphic processing units, Nvidia’s tech stack created lock-in that made it nearly impossible to switch.

The centerpiece of this strategy is the company’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, a proprietary software language optimized to run on the chips and achieve their best performance. Although the chips can be used without this specific software, the performance drop-off is steep, meaning that most AI applications require it.

Nvidia’s few competitors have tried to breach this barrier by designing software that more easily translates this language, but Nvidia maintains a powerful moat. In 2024, Nvidia updated its licensing agreements to disallow using the language on rival chips. The company also helps hyperscalers optimize their Nvidia stack, hiring engineers specifically for this purpose . As Nvidia executives noted during their most recent earnings call , “Customers can still mix and match. However, most companies just don’t have the skills to do that or a desire to do that.”

Nvidia’s strategy has borne fruit; the company enjoys a nearly 90 percent monopoly over the design market for graphics processing units. What’s more, Nvidia manages a 70-75 percent gross margin on the chips that it sells.

The power that Nvidia has amassed through this lock-in and its enormous stock price growth has allowed the corporation to begin functioning as, to use The New York Times’s phrase , “Silicon Valley’s central banker.” It has begun offering complex financing arrangements to partners, investing heavily in infrastructure that supports the use of its chips, such as neoclouds , and evaluating outside companies to acquire. Although Nvidia has long invested in AI startups, there has been a notable uptick in its deal activity in recent months.

By operating as an unregulated banker, Nvidia is shaping the U.S. economy outside the regulatory bounds intended to keep risky bets from collapsing the financial system — and the company has a vested interest in fueling the AI mania.

The more AI models that need to be trained faster, and the more data centers there are, the more Nvidia’s technology stack is being purchased and integrated into the American AI industry. But Nvidia’s hardware is expensive, so the company has begun offering complex financing arrangements to incentivize rapid adoption and compute purchases. These arrangements, of course, come with requirements to purchase Nvidia products and, often, to upgrade to the newest chips at regular intervals.

This is not the only deal structure Nvidia has piloted. The company has increasingly pursued a strategy of directly investing in neocloud infrastructure — data centers that rent cloud space to AI companies — and in turn requiring the neocloud companies to purchase a certain amount of Nvidia hardware and to upgrade it at a regular cadence. One of Nvidia’s biggest investments is in CoreWeave, of which it owns nearly 7 percent .

In late 2024, Nvidia completed an acquisition of Run:ai; in its most recent earnings call, the company announced commitments of $18 billion in equity investments for the remainder of the fiscal year, with its private company holdings almost doubling from 2025 to 2026. And in late August 2026, The Information reported Nvidia’s intention to acquire Hugging Face, a platform for open-source AI models, for $12.9 billion. Huang has noted that AI agents use “15-100x” the compute that a human using an AI model uses; it may be that Nvidia-owned Hugging Face begins preferencing agentic models, driving AI toward compute- and energy-heavy use cases (that benefit Nvidia).

In early August 2026, Nvidia announced a partnership with six private equity and investment bankers including Apollo, BlackRock, Goldman Sachs and KKR to “turn Nvidia compute and full-stack AI infrastructure into an investable asset class for global capital,” according to the press release. The partnership will pool capital and offer “attractive rates” for enterprises to invest in Nvidia infrastructure.

In other words, the AI bubble is now an asset for some of the biggest players on Wall Street, while Nvidia grows its bottom line.

The explosion of the AI industry and the vast amounts of capital sloshing through seem to have taken many political leaders by surprise. But in one sense, this is an old story: a powerful corporation with a near-monopoly on a valuable product has amassed enough capital to begin acting as an unregulated banker, putting the U.S. economy at risk. If AI demand fails to keep pace, Nvidia’s financial entanglements across the space become a massive liability.

It is time for Congress to investigate these financing practices, demand more transparent financial disclosures, and pass a ban on Nvidia’s (and others’) ability to move vertically through the tech stack through acquisition or other investment. Nvidia has become a corporate giant, and these steps alone may not curtail its march through the AI industry — but Silicon Valley’s unregulated bank must be brought to heel.

Olivia Kosloff is a senior fellow at the American Economic Liberties Project, where Colin Dunkley is a legal analyst.

articles.title: AI fears hammer Google parent’s stock, erasing $500 billion in value
articles.summary: Shares of Google parent company Alphabet sank by as much as 15.8%, on course for the company’s worst single-day drop in history.
articles.body: Shares of Google parent company Alphabet sank Thursday by more than 12%, in its worst one-day performance ever, wiping out more than $500 billion in market value. Alphabet is America’s fourth-largest company, worth a total of $3.42 trillion, as of midday. Still, the amount of value it shed Thursday ranks as the second-worst wipeout in market history, only behind Nvidia’s $589 billion drop in 2025. The sharp drop in its stock price Thursday was the latest sign of broader anxiety across Wall Street over how long it will take big artificial intelligence companies to see consistent returns on investments worth hundreds of billions of dollars. On Wednesday, Alphabet reported its latest quarterly financial results, revealing that revenues fell short of Wall Street’s expectations. It also reported lackluster advertising sales. The “magnitude” of the slowdown in Google’s search business was “steeper than expected,” JPMorgan Chase analysts wrote in a Thursday morning note. A senior Alphabet executive told investors Wednesday that part of the reason ad revenues from search were underperforming was because of Google’s own “AI Mode” search feature, which was resulting in fewer ads. The company is working on addressing this, senior vice president Philipp Schindler said on the investor call, adding that “ad experiments” in the feature have “shown promising results.” Company executives tried to soften the blow for investors by touting more than 1 billion users of its Gemini AI app. But all that AI is coming at a massive cost to Alphabet, which disclosed that it has committed to more than $1 trillion worth of multiyear spending agreements to fund the infrastructure, energy and leases required to run AI systems. The company said during its July earnings report that it planned to spend more than $200 billion this year, which is double what it spent in 2025. The company in June also raised almost $80 billion in capital, also to spend on the ever-expanding AI build-out. Alphabet’s disappointing results also came against the backdrop of better results from its peer Microsoft, whose shares initially rose in after-hours trading Wednesday and overnight before reversing course to fall about 1.5% by 1:20 p.m. ET Thursday. The big drop in Alphabet shares dragged down the Nasdaq Composite index, which was down 1.5% by the afternoon. The S&P 500 fell slightly less, by about 0.4%. Shares of chip companies that supply equipment for AI data centers followed Alphabet shares lower, with the Philadelphia semiconductor index dropping 1.6%. The bleeding even spread beyond the tech sector, as shares of construction equipment giant Caterpillar — a key supplier of the machines required to build data centers — plunged 9% early Thursday. Caterpillar’s recent earnings report revealed that the company’s revenues beat Wall Street expectations but by less than many traders had hoped. The industrial giant was the second worst performing stock on Thursday in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, behind only Alphabet. The Dow declined slightly more than 200 points. As investors clamor for ever-higher returns from companies linked to the costly AI build-out, stock in firms that only narrowly top earnings targets, like Caterpillar, has been punished with dramatic sell-offs.

articles.title: SEC Eyes Manipulation, Insider Risk in Prediction Markets
articles.summary: Add another regulator to the list of watchdogs monitoring risks in the fast-growing prediction market industry: the Securities and Exchange Commission.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Add another regulator to the list of watchdogs monitoring risks in the fast-growing prediction market industry: the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Trades tied to companies' key performance indicators or earnings measures can fall under the Wall Street regulator's turf and SEC Enforcement Director David Woodcock said the agency is watching out for signs of foul play.

"We're following that very closely," Woodcock said in an interview with Bloomberg. "We have to be ready to act when people are committing fraud or committing other securities violations, and I think we are going to be. I suspect you will see activity in that space."

Insider trading and market manipulation are the SEC's main concerns, Woodcock said, adding that enforcement activity is likely "in the future, for sure."

Oversight of prediction markets like Kalshi and the US arm of Polymarket largely falls to the smaller Washington financial regulator, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which views the platforms' wagers on everything from sports to elections as financial swaps under its purview.

That agency has brought several prediction market enforcement cases so far this year. Former Congressman George Santos agreed to pay more than $35,000 to settle allegations he manipulated Kalshi wagers and a White House teleprompter operator settled with the CFTC over allegedly using insider information to rack up wins on Kalshi.

In April, the CFTC and federal prosecutors alleged a US soldier used classified information about the timing of the capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to make more than $400,000 on Polymarket. That case is ongoing and the soldier has pleaded not guilty.

Kalshi and Polymarket have said they are against insider trading, monitor their platforms for potential risks and flag suspicious activities to regulators.

The CFTC views the platforms as derivative exchanges but some states argue prediction markets are illegal gambling operations shirking local laws. That has led to a high-stakes legal fight that will likely end up at the US Supreme Court.

Trading products become the SEC's turf when they are tied to securities. The agency put out a joint request for comment with the CFTC on the definitions of certain swaps and derivatives products as part of a bid to clarify the two agencies' jurisdictions.

articles.title: Finland launches criminal probe of suspected environmental damage by Google
articles.summary: The US tech giant is investing $15bn in a huge new data centre project in northern Finland.
articles.body:
Finnish police have launched a criminal investigation into suspected breaches of environmental law at the construction site of a planned Google data centre in northern Finland.

The project is part of a $15bn deal announced last month by Alphabet’s Google to invest in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure in Finland, which the US company described as its largest investment in Europe.

Authorities have said Tuike Finland, a local subsidiary of Google, conducted forest clearing and drainage at a planned site near the town of Muhos, before the environmental impact assessments required under Finnish law had been completed.

“We are investigating whether the company’s operations have breached the Water Act and resulted in environmental damage,” Detective Superintendent Kari Pakanen told the Reuters news agency on Thursday, adding that a guilty finding could lead to a corporate fine.

Pakanen declined to say whether any individuals could become a target of the investigation, and a Google spokesperson said the company would cooperate with the police investigation and continue to focus on maintaining compliance at its sites.

Videos and photographs showing the scale of the forest clearance at the site of the data centre, and Google’s initial reluctance to address the issue in the days after the news broke, have prompted widespread anger in Finland, where there is a high level of respect for the natural environment among the public.

“All the outrage and dismay directed at Google, I can very much share that, especially when we are talking about the parent company valued as the third-largest in the world,” Finnish Green MP Oras Tynkkynen told Al Jazeera. “There is just no excuse. You have to know the legislation of the country you are operating in; you can afford to hire the best legal experts to help you navigate the local legal requirements.”

Finnish authorities ordered Google to stop work at the data centre site at the start of October, and the latest information from the police highlights shortcomings in the drainage and water management at the site.

Tynkkynen called Google’s actions “unforgivable”, but cautioned that while the anger being directed at the US tech giant was justified, it was also diverting scrutiny away from legacy Finnish forestry companies, which he says are “by far the biggest contributors to biodiversity loss in this country”.

What is Finland’s appeal for data centre construction?

Finland’s cool climate, low-carbon electricity and government endorsement of AI projects have contributed to making the country one of Europe’s main destinations for data centre investments in recent years.

Finland, similar in size to Germany – but with one-seventh of the population, less than six million people – has had less vocal opposition to data centre buildouts than other places, including in the United States.

AI data centres are among the main drivers of a projected rise of up to 40 percent in Finland’s electricity consumption in the coming years, if all agreed grid connection projects go ahead, grid operator Fingrid has said.

Google’s planned investments in Finland include data centres, electricity grid improvements and clean energy and battery projects to power services such as Gemini, Search, Maps and YouTube.

Supporting Google’s plan, Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in September that the deal would be a boost for the economy, playing down concerns that it would suck up energy and push up power prices.

articles.title: Caterpillar, the Dow's best stock of 2026, is unraveling — and an earnings beat couldn't stop it
articles.summary: Caterpillar topped earnings estimates, but the Dow's best stock of 2026 is sinking anyway as Wall Street keeps dumping stocks tied to the AI build-out.
articles.body:
Wall Street is still dumping stocks tied to the AI build-out, and an earnings beat offers no protection. Caterpillar ( CAT ) topped estimates and is sinking anyway.

The heavy-equipment maker, which sells power-generation gear to data centers, posted third quarter adjusted profit above forecasts and a record backlog of about $78 billion. But tariff refunds helped the profit number, revenue was roughly in line, and the company guided to only "moderate" sales growth in the fourth quarter.

That wasn't enough for a stock priced for more. Caterpillar is on track for its worst day since March 2020, two weeks before stocks hit their pandemic lows, and its lowest close since January.

The fall is steep, a mirror of its ascent. Caterpillar was the best-performing stock in the Dow ( ^DJI ) for about half of this year, according to Yahoo Finance calculations, and finished June up 86%, far ahead of any other member.

It hasn't held the top spot since early October. Thursday's drop leaves the stock nearly 40% below its June record and its 2026 gain in the middle of the pack, well behind new leader Chevron ( CVX ).

The selloff has erased more than $190 billion in market value from Caterpillar's peak.

Some investors were already heading for the exits before the report. Todd Sohn, managing director and chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas, found that investors have been pulling cash from funds that hold economically sensitive stocks like Caterpillar and moving it into safer areas such as healthcare and utilities.

That kind of retreat is rare with the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) so close to its record, Sohn wrote in a Tuesday note, and it means expectations for those stocks are already low. "It's a low bar for cyclical areas to bounce back," he wrote.

Thursday's drop has already carried Caterpillar through its February and March lows near $665, and the stock is now approaching potential support around $625, where buyers stepped in back in January. If that gives way, the next floor sits near $540, a level that would erase the stock's entire 2026 gain.

articles.title: Polymarket halts trading for an hour after vendor compromise, says impacted users will be ‘made whole’
articles.summary: Predictions markets platform Polymarket was forced to halt trading on its international platform for an hour after a vendor was compromised.
articles.body: Predictions markets platform Polymarket was forced to halt trading on its international platform Thursday for nearly an hour because of what it said was a compromise of third-party software. There were also unconfirmed reports from users on Polymarket’s Discord channel who said their wallets had been drained. While Polymarket did not confirm that users had lost money, it said in an X post that “anyone who has been impacted will be made whole.” “We’ll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders,” the company said in a subsequent post on X. Polymarket said the attack appeared to be emanating from the United Kingdom, and that it had referred the matter to British law enforcement authorities. The hackers gained access to the funds via software from DebugBear, a web analytics and website performance tool, according to a person familiar with the details who was granted anonymity to address an evolving security situation. DebugBear had said on X that it was experiencing an “ongoing security incident” at around 2 p.m. ET Thursday. Crypto news website The Block reported that some $2.65 million in cryptocurrencies had been siphoned from Polymarket users’ wallets, citing data from blockchain analysis group Arkham. A Polymarket representative declined to comment on that figure or on the precise nature of the attack. Polymarket said in its X post that it had identified and fixed an issue affecting its international platform, Polymarket.com. “One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement,” Polymarket said. “Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading & are working to bring the platform back online,” it added. Trading began again at 3 p.m. ET after nearly an hour offline. Polymarket’s U.S.-based platform did not appear to be affected by the breach. Compromising third party vendors has become a very common way malicious actors gain access to large platforms and websites. That these hackers succeeded in stealing money from Polymarket’s users, however, makes this a significant breach. Polymarket was valued at $21 billion in September after a group of investors led by Donald Trump Jr. invested $1 billion into the platform. The company currently processes approximately $200 million worth of trading activity daily. Polymarket, along with rival Kalshi, has become the subject of an intense, multi-million-dollar battle between U.S. states and the Trump administration over who gets to regulate the prediction-market betting that occurs on the sites. The platforms also continue to fight off insider-trading threats. Earlier Thursday, Bloomberg News reported Polymarket was investigating reports of suspicious bets made amid Israel’s closely watched elections. It is also investigating “dozens” related to the U.S. midterms, according to the company’s head of global intelligence and investigations, Shana Bautista. Earlier this month, Kalshi said it was looking into suspicious bets involving Trump’s choice of press secretary.
